question: to the Commission Sofie Eriksson (S&D), Heléne Fritzon (S&D) Subject:

The Baltic Sea was identified as an urgent priority in the European Ocean Pact and the Commission organised the high-level ‘Our Baltic’ event in 2025. This event was presented as the starting point for a renewed and more holistic approach to addressing the serious challenges facing the Baltic Sea, including ecosystem degradation, pollution from land and sea and the need for more sustainable fisheries management. Since the ‘Our Baltic’ event, Parliament has adopted its own-initiative report on the Baltic Sea, thereby making its ambitions and expectations of the Commission very clear. However, it remains unclear what concrete next steps the Commission intends to take. 1.
What concrete actions does the Commission intend to take going forward to address ecosystem challenges, pollution, and fisheries management in the Baltic Sea?

In the light of the recently published advice of the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES), does the Commission intend to advocate for lower fishing quotas in the Baltic Sea next year? Please answer yes or no.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) 1. The Commission is cooperating with Member States to improve the implementation of the EU environmental legislation, notably the Marine Strategy Framework Directive1 to achieve good environmental status. Within the Helsinki Convention for the Baltic the European Union supports regional commitments to achieve the same goal. The Commission also reinforces the EU’s zero-pollution agenda by targeting nutrient pollution, hazardous chemicals and marine litter, focussing on enforcing rules to reduce pollution at source, as through the evaluation of the Nitrate Directive2 and the revised Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive3. In parallel, the Commission is strengthening the science and knowledge base for action by improving ocean research, data and knowledge through initiatives like OceanEye4. This is intended to support better-informed decisions on pollution, biodiversity and climate, alongside work on an Ocean and Water Research and Innovation Strategy. As regards fisheries management, with the ‘Baltic project’ the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea, its partners and the Commission services work on further improving the scientific advice by widening the considerations covered. A first concrete step is a threeyear research project which aims to build the scientific and operational foundation for ecosystem-based fisheries management in the western Baltic Sea. Moreover, the Commission is committed to continue the rebuilding trajectories for the fishers. 2. For its proposal on the Baltic fishing opportunities for 2027, the Commission will consider all relevant aspects, including ecosystem-based approach to fisheries management, as set out in Article 2 of the Regulation establishing the Common Fisheries Policy5.
